Membership Filtering — Methodology

Methodology · Gaia DR3 globular-cluster membership

Finding a cluster's true stars in a crowd of millions.

A globular cluster sits behind a dense screen of unrelated foreground and background stars. This is the step-by-step method we use to decide, for every star Gaia sees, whether it truly belongs to the cluster — using how it moves, where it sits, and its colour, because distance alone cannot tell them apart.

Pick target + region→ Download & clean→ Motion→ Position→ Colour→ Membership probability
174,486
stars examined in the Omega Centauri field

3
independent tests every star must satisfy

Why distance can't do it alone

The obvious idea — "keep the stars at the cluster's distance" — fails. Gaia measures distance through parallax, and at a globular cluster's distance the measurement error is larger than the signal for all but a few percent of stars. So instead of one unreliable clue we combine three reliable ones. A real member betrays itself three ways at once, and our filter scores each.

01

Aim at the cluster and set the search region

Define where to look

From a catalogue we take each cluster's centre (right ascension & declination) and its tidal radius — the edge beyond which the Milky Way's gravity strips stars away. We search a circle of exactly that radius, so we capture the whole cluster without dragging in more field than necessary.

Two clusters had a broken catalogue radius (a formula that misfires for collapsed cores); we replaced those with measured literature values so the circle wasn't accidentally cut inside the cluster.

region: circle of radius = tidal radius  ·  centre: Harris catalogue RA/Dec
02

Download the stars and throw out the bad measurements

Clean the data

We pull every star in that circle from Gaia DR3 with its position, motion, brightness and colour. Before any science we discard stars whose measurements can't be trusted: poorly-fit astrometry, noisy motions, and anything too faint to measure well.

We also drop obvious foreground stars — ones whose parallax places them clearly in front of the cluster (more than 3σ nearer than expected). This is the one safe use of parallax: not to pin a distance, just to reject the certain intruders.

RUWE < 1.4  ·  motion error < 1.5 mas/yr  ·  brightness G < 20.5  ·  reject parallax > 3σ in front
03

Motion — the strongest clue

Do the stars move together?

Cluster stars orbit the galaxy as one group, so on the sky they all drift the same direction at the same speed (their "proper motion"). Field stars drift every which way. Plot every star's motion and the cluster appears as a tight clump; the field is a broad smear.

We fit that clump with a statistical model anchored to the cluster's known mean motion, so it can never lock onto the wrong crowd. Each star gets a probability from how deep inside the clump it falls, folding in its own measurement error. Stars far outside are cut immediately.

pmotion = exp( −½ · [ (ΔpmRA / σ)² + (ΔpmDec / σ)² ] )
04

Position — do they cluster in space?

Are they concentrated?

A cluster is a ball of stars, densest at its centre and thinning outward in a characteristic King profile. Field stars are spread evenly. We fit that profile to the star counts, and each star gets a score for how cluster-dominated its neighbourhood is.

Rather than multiplying probabilities, we use position as context: near the crowded centre a star needs less convincing; in the sparse outskirts it needs a decisive motion. If Gaia can't resolve a cluster's packed core, this test steps aside and the decision rests on motion alone.

density(r) = amp · [ (1 + (r/rc)²)−½ − edge ]² + background
05

Colour — were they born together?

Do they share one family sequence?

Cluster stars formed at the same time from the same cloud, so on a colour–brightness diagram they trace a single narrow track (main sequence, giant branch, horizontal branch). Unrelated field stars scatter all over it.

We build that track empirically from the stars already looking like members, then score every star by how close it sits to it. For clusters seen through patchy interstellar dust — which smears the track — this test is down-weighted or switched off, since a blurred ridge would punish real members.

06

Combine the three into one probability

Decide, and record the odds

The three tests are combined by probability, not a simple AND. Motion sets the base odds; position nudges them up or down by how cluster-dominated the star's surroundings are; colour applies a final factor. The result is a single membership probability from 0 to 1 for every star.

Stars above the threshold (usually 0.5) are flagged as members and carried into the science. Nothing is a hard yes/no black box — every star keeps its probability, so later analysis can tighten or loosen the cut and see the effect.

output per star: pmotion · pposition · pcolour → membership_prob → is_member

One method, tuned per cluster

The same three tests run for every cluster, but their settings adapt to the environment — a lone halo cluster and one buried in the galactic bulge are not the same problem.

EnvironmentExampleWhat changesColour test
cleanOmega Cen, M3High-latitude, simple field — standard motion clump & all three tests.full
crowdedM4, Terzan 5Bulge/disk field — stricter motion gate, extra field component modelled.off / low
companion47 Tuc, NGC 362A second galaxy (the SMC) in frame — an extra population is fitted so it isn't mistaken for members.full
sparsePalomar 5Too few stars to model — a direct motion window around the known value.half
distantNGC 2419So far that motions are error-dominated — an error-aware window and a gentler threshold.full
Each cluster's result is saved as a star table with a membership_prob and is_member for every star, feeding the rotation, V/σ and tidal-stripping analyses. Source: Gaia DR3; mean motions anchored to Vasiliev & Baumgardt (2021). Figures generated from the project's own filtered Omega Centauri and NGC 288 catalogues.
